title: By what authority? (Mark 11:27–33)
hookLine: leaders try to trap him, and he answers with a question

cards: "Have you stopped being late all the time?" Some questions aren't really questions. Whatever you say, you lose.
Jesus is back in Jerusalem, walking in the temple courts, the day after he overturned the tables. A delegation arrives: the chief priests, the scribes and the elders.

In the King James Bible they ask: "By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority to do these things?" It's a trap with two jaws. Say God gave it to me, and they could call it blasphemy.
Say no one, and he's just a troublemaker from Galilee. And the crowd is listening.

teach.h: LET ME ASK YOU ONE QUESTION.
teach.b: Jesus says: let me ask you one question. Answer me, and I'll tell you by what authority I do these things.

teach.h: JOHN: FROM HEAVEN, OR OF MEN?
teach.b: "The baptism of John, was it from heaven, or of men? answer me." Now they're the ones in the trap. They huddle.
If we say from heaven, he'll say, then why didn't you believe him? If we say from men, the crowd will turn on us, because, as Mark puts it, all men counted John a prophet indeed.
So they give the safest answer there is: "We cannot tell." And Jesus says: "Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things." This isn't a dodge.
His question and theirs are the same question. John had baptized him, and the voice from heaven spoke at that very moment. If they could be honest about John, they'd have their answer about Jesus.
Jesus answers with a question again and again in the Gospels. Who do you say I am?

teach.h: NEITHER DO I TELL YOU BY WHAT AUTHORITY.
teach.b: What do you want? Why are you afraid? A good question doesn't close the conversation.
It hands it back and asks you to be honest. Mark lets us overhear what the leaders weigh: the crowd, not John. The word for authority in Greek is exousia: the right, and the power, to act.

how: Christians often notice how many questions Jesus asks in the Gospels, and some Bible study groups use his questions, like "who do you say I am?", as prompts for honest discussion.

o: a teacher's skill at clever debate
the right and the power to act
a crowd's loud cheer of approval

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus refused to answer because he had no answer
his question about John was the answer, if they'd been honest.
everyone held John to have been a real prophet.
the leaders talked it over before they answered
Mark lets us hear them reason: if we say from heaven... if we say of men...

games.q: you're a leader who has asked Jesus: by what authority? he asks back: was John's baptism from heaven, or of men? the crowd is listening. what do you say?
games.why: they choose "We cannot tell." and he replies: "Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things."

practice: Think of a hard question someone's been pressing on you, at work, at home, or in your own head, and instead of rushing to answer, ask what question lies underneath: what are you really asking, what would help, what do you think, what are you afraid of?
Find one honest question you could hand back, not to escape, but to open things up. If you pray, you can bring God your own hardest question.

wordCard.voice: Exousia, the Greek word for authority, the right and the power to act. The leaders' trap, answered with a question about John that they were afraid to answer honestly.

orig.note: Greek: authority, the right and power to act. the word in the leaders' question in Mark 11:28.

carryVoice: Your line: answer with a question. A good one hands the conversation back. Until tomorrow.
